claim: Spike timing-dependent plasticity (STDP) is under neuromodulatory control, which is correlated with distinct behavioral states.
source: Spike timing-dependent plasticity (STDP) is under neuromodulatory control, which is correlated with distinct behavioral states.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general principle underlying the study.

claim: Dopamine, a reward signal, broadens the time window for synaptic potentiation.
source: Previously, we reported that dopamine, a reward signal, broadens the time window for synaptic potentiation and modulates the outcome of hippocampal STDP even when applied after the plasticity induction protocol (Brzosko et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Dopamine modulates the outcome of hippocampal STDP even when applied after the plasticity induction protocol.
source: Previously, we reported that dopamine, a reward signal, broadens the time window for synaptic potentiation and modulates the outcome of hippocampal STDP even when applied after the plasticity induction protocol (Brzosko et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Acetylcholine biases STDP toward synaptic depression in mouse hippocampal slices.
source: Specifically, our experimental data in mouse hippocampal slices show that acetylcholine biases STDP toward synaptic depression, whilst subsequent application of dopamine converts this depression into potentiation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript (Figure 1).

claim: Subsequent application of dopamine converts acetylcholine-induced synaptic depression into potentiation.
source: Specifically, our experimental data in mouse hippocampal slices show that acetylcholine biases STDP toward synaptic depression, whilst subsequent application of dopamine converts this depression into potentiation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript (Figure 2).

claim: Incorporating bidirectional neuromodulation-enabled correlational synaptic learning rule into a computational model yields effective navigation toward changing reward locations.
source: Incorporating this bidirectional neuromodulation-enabled correlational synaptic learning rule into a computational model yields effective navigation toward changing reward locations, as in natural foraging behavior.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results presented in Figure 4.

claim: Temporally sequenced neuromodulation of STDP enables associations to be made between actions and outcomes.
source: Thus, temporally sequenced neuromodulation of STDP enables associations to be made between actions and outcomes and also provides a possible mechanism for aligning the time scales of cellular and behavioral learning.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental and computational results.

claim: Temporally sequenced neuromodulation of STDP provides a possible mechanism for aligning the time scales of cellular and behavioral learning.
source: Thus, temporally sequenced neuromodulation of STDP enables associations to be made between actions and outcomes and also provides a possible mechanism for aligning the time scales of cellular and behavioral learning.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental and computational results.

claim: STDP is a form of Hebbian learning that depends on the order and precise timing of presynaptic and postsynaptic spikes.
source: Spike timing-dependent plasticity (STDP) is a form of Hebbian learning that depends on the order and precise timing of presynaptic and postsynaptic spikes (Gerstner et al., 1996; Markram et al., 1997; Bi and Poo, 1998; Song et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to foundational work on STDP.

claim: STDP has been implicated in several forms of learning and memory including competitive Hebbian learning.
source: STDP is a computationally attractive mechanism that has been implicated in several forms of learning and memory including competitive Hebbian learning (Song et al., 2000; Clopath et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous computational and experimental work.

claim: Conventional STDP is unsupervised, meaning the resulting plasticity is not informed by the outcome of the activity.
source: Firstly, in contrast to many forms of behavioral learning, conventional STDP is unsupervised, that is, the resulting plasticity is not informed by the outcome of the activity (Hertz et al., 1991; Gerstner et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical work on learning.

claim: STDP relies on shorter time scales than most behaviors.
source: Secondly, STDP relies on shorter time scales than most behaviors.
evidence: This is a known property of STDP compared to behavioral timescales.

claim: STDP is under neuromodulatory influence.
source: Given that STDP is under neuromodulatory influence (Seol et al., 2007; Zhang et al., 2009; Pawlak et al., 2010), here we sought to determine whether behaviorally relevant activation of different neuromodulatory signals could address both of these issues in hippocampus-dependent learning.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous experimental work.

claim: The hippocampus with its constituent place cells has been implicated in spatial learning and memory in non-human animals.
source: A wealth of experimental data has implicated the hippocampus with its constituent place cells (O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971; O'Keefe and Nadel, 1978) in spatial learning and memory in non-human animals (Morris et al., 1982) as well as humans (Ekstrom et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to foundational work on hippocampal function.

claim: The hippocampus with its constituent place cells has been implicated in spatial learning and memory in humans.
source: A wealth of experimental data has implicated the hippocampus with its constituent place cells (O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971; O'Keefe and Nadel, 1978) in spatial learning and memory in non-human animals (Morris et al., 1982) as well as humans (Ekstrom et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to work on human hippocampal function.

claim: Hippocampal synaptic plasticity, including STDP, is believed to mediate the encoding of spatial memories.
source: Hippocampal synaptic plasticity (Bliss and Lomo, 1973; Bliss and Collingridge, 1993), including STDP (Bi and Poo, 1998; Debanne et al., 1998; Kwag and Paulsen, 2009; Andrade-Talavera et al., 2016), is believed to mediate the encoding of spatial memories (Morris et al., 1986; Tsien et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to work on hippocampal plasticity and memory.

claim: Different neuromodulatory inputs into the hippocampus are active during distinct behavioral states.
source: Different neuromodulatory inputs into the hippocampus are active during distinct behavioral states.
evidence: This is a general principle supported by the specific examples that follow.

claim: Exploratory behavior coincides with an increased cholinergic tone.
source: In particular, whilst exploratory behavior coincides with an increased cholinergic tone (Kametani and Kawamura, 1990; Marrosu et al., 1995; Thiel et al., 1998), rewards are associated with activity of dopaminergic neurons (Schultz et al., 1997; Suri and Schultz, 1999; Pan et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous experimental work.

claim: Rewards are associated with activity of dopaminergic neurons.
source: In particular, whilst exploratory behavior coincides with an increased cholinergic tone (Kametani and Kawamura, 1990; Marrosu et al., 1995; Thiel et al., 1998), rewards are associated with activity of dopaminergic neurons (Schultz et al., 1997; Suri and Schultz, 1999; Pan et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous experimental work.

claim: Dopamine can convert hippocampal timing-dependent long-term depression (t-LTD) into timing-dependent long-term potentiation (t-LTP) when applied after a delay of minutes.
source: Importantly, we recently demonstrated that dopamine can convert hippocampal timing-dependent long-term depression (t-LTD) into timing-dependent long-term potentiation (t-LTP) when applied after a delay of minutes (Brzosko et al., 2015), thus providing a possible mechanism for a supervisory signal to associate specific experiences with delayed rewards in hippocampus-dependent reward learning.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Pre-before-post pairing with a time interval of 10 ms induced t-LTP in control condition.
source: Consistent with previous studies (Bi and Poo, 1998; Zhang et al., 2009; Edelmann and Lessmann, 2011; Brzosko et al., 2015), in control condition the pre-before-post pairing with a time interval between the presynaptic and postsynaptic activity (Δt) of 10 ms induced t-LTP (+ Pairing – ACh: 135 ± 7%, t(7) = 4.7, p=0.0022 vs. 100%, n = 8; Figure 1a,b; Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 and consistent with previous studies.

claim: When acetylcholine (1 μM) was bath-applied during pre-before-post pairing with Δt = 10 ms, robust t-LTD was induced.
source: However, when acetylcholine (1 μM) was bath-applied for 10 min from 1 to 2 min before and during the same pre-before-post pairing in interleaved experiments, robust t-LTD was induced (+ Pairing + ACh: 63 ± 8%, t(5) = 4.9, p=0.0046 vs. 100%, n = 6; t(12) = 6.6, p<0.0001 vs. + Pairing – ACh; Figure 1a,b; Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Application of acetylcholine for 10 min had no significant effect on the basal Schaffer collateral transmission without pairing with postsynaptic action potentials.
source: In accordance with earlier reports (Sugisaki et al., 2011), application of acetylcholine for 10 min had no significant effect on the basal Schaffer collateral transmission (– Pairing + ACh: 90 ± 6%, t(6) = 1.8, p=0.1220 vs. 100%, n = 7; Figure 1a,b; Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 and consistent with previous reports.

claim: Muscarinic acetylcholine receptors are highly expressed in the hippocampus.
source: Since muscarinic acetylcholine receptors are highly expressed in the hippocampus (Levey et al., 1995), the specificity of this cholinergic modulation of STDP was assessed using the muscarinic acetylcholine receptor antagonist atropine (100 nM).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The application of atropine prevented acetylcholine-facilitated t-LTD, resulting in significant t-LTP instead.
source: The application of atropine prevented acetylcholine-facilitated t-LTD, resulting in significant t-LTP instead (Δt =+10 ms; +ACh: 63 ± 9%, t(4) = 4.1, p=0.0146 vs. 100%, n = 5; +ACh + Atropine: 141 ± 8%, t(5) = 5.1, p=0.0037 vs. 100%, n = 6; t(9) = 6.5, p<0.0001 vs. +ACh; Figure 1c,d; Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The facilitation of t-LTD was due to specific muscarinic acetylcholine receptor activation.
source: This implies that the facilitation of t-LTD was due to specific muscarinic acetylcholine receptor activation.
evidence: This is inferred from the atropine blocking experiment.

claim: Input-specific t-LTD was induced when acetylcholine was applied during the pairing protocol with Δt = 0 ms.
source: Input-specific t-LTD was also induced when acetylcholine was applied during the pairing protocol with Δt = 0 ms (Control: 160 ± 17%, t(4) = 3.6, p=0.0238 vs. 100%, n = 5; + ACh: 64 ± 13%, t(7) = 2.9, p=0.0245 vs. 100%, n = 8; t(4) = 5.9, p=0.0041 vs. Control; Figure 1e; Figure 1—source data 1; unpaired control pathway not shown)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: Input-specific t-LTD was induced when acetylcholine was applied during the pairing protocol with Δt = −20 ms.
source: Input-specific t-LTD was also induced when acetylcholine was applied during the pairing protocol with Δt = 0 ms (Control: 160 ± 17%, t(4) = 3.6, p=0.0238 vs. 100%, n = 5; + ACh: 64 ± 13%, t(7) = 2.9, p=0.0245 vs. 100%, n = 8; t(4) = 5.9, p=0.0041 vs. Control; Figure 1e; Figure 1—source data 1; unpaired control pathway not shown) and Δt = −20 ms (Control: 66 ± 10%, t(6) = 3.5, p=0.0124 vs. 100%, n = 7; + ACh: 63 ± 12%, t(5) = 3.0, p=0.0292 vs. 100%, n = 6; t(5) = 0.7, p=0.5265 vs. Control; Figure 1e; Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: Pairing protocols with spike timing interval extended to ±50 ms during application of acetylcholine did not lead to a significant change in synaptic weights.
source: However, pairing protocols with spike timing interval extended to ±50 ms during application of acetylcholine did not lead to a significant change in synaptic weights (Δt =+50 ms: 84 ± 11%, t(6) = 1.5, p=0.1852 vs. 100%, n = 7; Δt = −50 ms: 113 ± 15%, t(5) = 0.8, p=0.4409 vs. 100%, n = 6; Figure 1e; Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: The activation of muscarinic acetylcholine receptors during coordinated spiking activity biases STDP toward synaptic depression at the Schaffer collateral pathway.
source: Together, our results suggest that the activation of muscarinic acetylcholine receptors during the coordinated spiking activity biases STDP toward synaptic depression at the Schaffer collateral pathway.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results in Figure 1.

claim: Both dopamine and acetylcholine modulate synaptic plasticity to yield synaptic potentiation and depression, respectively, irrespective of the precise spike order during pairing.
source: Hence, both dopamine (Brzosko et al., 2015) and acetylcholine (Figure 1) modulate synaptic plasticity to yield synaptic potentiation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a,c; Figure 1—source data 2; Brzosko et al., 2015) and depression (Figure 1e), respectively, irrespective of the precise spike order during pairing.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 and previous work.

claim: Each of the two neuromodulators effectively converts a spike timing-dependent learning rule into a correlation-based learning rule but they do so in opposite directions.
source: Each of the two neuromodulators effectively converts a spike timing-dependent learning rule into a correlation-based learning rule but they do so in opposite directions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: Co-activation of dopaminergic and cholinergic receptors results in synaptic depression with post-before-pre pairing.
source: We found that co-activation of dopaminergic and cholinergic receptors results in synaptic depression with post-before-pre pairing and leads to an initial synaptic depression followed by a gradual reversal of the synaptic weights back toward baseline with pre-before-post pairing (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b,c; Figure 1—source data 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Co-activation of dopaminergic and cholinergic receptors leads to an initial synaptic depression followed by a gradual reversal of the synaptic weights back toward baseline with pre-before-post pairing.
source: We found that co-activation of dopaminergic and cholinergic receptors results in synaptic depression with post-before-pre pairing and leads to an initial synaptic depression followed by a gradual reversal of the synaptic weights back toward baseline with pre-before-post pairing (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b,c; Figure 1—source data 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Acetylcholine, primarily via activation of muscarinic M1 receptors, facilitates hippocampal LTP in several previous studies using plasticity induction protocols other than STDP.
source: While several previous studies using plasticity induction protocols other than STDP showed that acetylcholine, primarily via activation of muscarinic M1 receptors, facilitates hippocampal LTP (Boddeke et al., 1992; Huerta and Lisman, 1995; Ovsepian et al., 2004; Shinoe et al., 2005; Buchanan et al., 2010; Connor et al., 2012; Digby et al., 2012; Dennis et al., 2016), acetylcholine has also been found to induce LTD, particularly at higher concentrations (Scheiderer et al., 2006; Volk et al., 2007; Dickinson et al., 2009; Jo et al., 2010; Kamsler et al., 2010) — likely through the activation of a number of muscarinic receptor subtypes (Teles-Grilo Ruivo and Mellor, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Acetylcholine has been found to induce LTD, particularly at higher concentrations.
source: While several previous studies using plasticity induction protocols other than STDP showed that acetylcholine, primarily via activation of muscarinic M1 receptors, facilitates hippocampal LTP (Boddeke et al., 1992; Huerta and Lisman, 1995; Ovsepian et al., 2004; Shinoe et al., 2005; Buchanan et al., 2010; Connor et al., 2012; Digby et al., 2012; Dennis et al., 2016), acetylcholine has also been found to induce LTD, particularly at higher concentrations (Scheiderer et al., 2006; Volk et al., 2007; Dickinson et al., 2009; Jo et al., 2010; Kamsler et al., 2010) — likely through the activation of a number of muscarinic receptor subtypes (Teles-Grilo Ruivo and Mellor, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: The polarity of acetylcholine-modulated plasticity can depend on the concentration of agonist used and specific cholinergic receptor subtype activated.
source: Thus, the polarity of acetylcholine-modulated plasticity can depend on the concentration of agonist used and specific cholinergic receptor subtype activated (Müller et al., 1988; Auerbach and Segal, 1996; Dennis et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: A lower concentration of acetylcholine (100 nM) during pre-before-post pairing did not result in synaptic depression, but it prevented significant potentiation from developing.
source: Under our experimental conditions, a lower concentration of acetylcholine (100 nM) during pre-before-post pairing did not result in synaptic depression, but it prevented significant potentiation from developing (Δt =+10 ms; − ACh: 162 ± 16%, t(5) = 3.8, p=0.0127 vs. 100%, n = 6; + ACh: 113 ± 9%, t(9) = 1.4, p=0.1888 vs. 100%, n = 10; t(14) = 2.9, p=0.0119 vs. − ACh; Figure 1—figure supplement 2; Figure 1—source data 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The findings are consistent with previous reports using STDP induction protocols, showing that cholinergic receptor activation enables t-LTD in the visual cortex.
source: Our findings are consistent with previous reports using STDP induction protocols, showing that cholinergic receptor activation enables t-LTD in the visual cortex (Seol et al., 2007) and facilitates t-LTD in the dorsal cochlear nucleus (Zhao and Tzounopoulos, 2011), but appear to contrast with results from studies in the rat hippocampus (Adams et al., 2004; Sugisaki et al., 2011, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The findings are consistent with previous reports using STDP induction protocols, showing that cholinergic receptor activation facilitates t-LTD in the dorsal cochlear nucleus.
source: Our findings are consistent with previous reports using STDP induction protocols, showing that cholinergic receptor activation enables t-LTD in the visual cortex (Seol et al., 2007) and facilitates t-LTD in the dorsal cochlear nucleus (Zhao and Tzounopoulos, 2011), but appear to contrast with results from studies in the rat hippocampus (Adams et al., 2004; Sugisaki et al., 2011, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The findings appear to contrast with results from studies in the rat hippocampus.
source: Our findings are consistent with previous reports using STDP induction protocols, showing that cholinergic receptor activation enables t-LTD in the visual cortex (Seol et al., 2007) and facilitates t-LTD in the dorsal cochlear nucleus (Zhao and Tzounopoulos, 2011), but appear to contrast with results from studies in the rat hippocampus (Adams et al., 2004; Sugisaki et al., 2011, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Most reinforcement learning models rely on the ability of the reinforcing signal to strengthen active synapses, also when it arrives after the activity has occurred.
source: Most reinforcement learning models rely on the ability of the reinforcing signal to strengthen active synapses, also when it arrives after the activity has occurred (Sutton and Barto, 1981).
evidence: This is supported by citation to foundational work on reinforcement learning.

claim: Bath-application of atropine (100 nM) to block muscarinic acetylcholine receptors immediately after acetylcholine washout did not affect the expression of acetylcholine-facilitated t-LTD.
source: Bath-application of atropine (100 nM) to block muscarinic acetylcholine receptors immediately after acetylcholine washout did not affect the expression of acetylcholine-facilitated t-LTD (Δt =+10 ms; 79 ± 9%, t(9) = 2.4, p=0.0399 vs. 100%, n = 10; Figure 2a,c; Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Atropine did not significantly affect baseline EPSPs.
source: Atropine also did not significantly affect baseline EPSPs (83 ± 8%, t(6) = 2.2, p=0.0747 vs. 100%, n = 7; Figure 2c; Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: When dopamine (100 μM) was added to the superfusion fluid in the presence of atropine (100 nM) within 1 min after the pairing protocol, it converted acetylcholine-facilitated t-LTD into t-LTP.
source: Notably, when, in the presence of atropine (100 nM) to prevent sustained muscarinic receptor activation, dopamine (100 μM) was added to the superfusion fluid, for 10–12 min starting within 1 min after the pairing protocol in interleaved experiments, it converted acetylcholine-facilitated t-LTD into t-LTP (Δt =+10 ms; ACh + Atropine + DA: 145 ± 15%, t(6) = 3.0, p=0.0244 vs. 100%, n = 7; t(15) = 4.0, p=0.0011 vs. ACh + Atropine; Figure 2a,c; Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The adenylyl cyclase activator forskolin (50 μM), applied for 10–12 min immediately after the pairing protocol with Δt =+10 ms, resulted in robust conversion of acetylcholine-facilitated t-LTD into t-LTP, emulating the effect of dopamine.
source: Similarly, the adenylyl cyclase activator forskolin (50 μM), applied for 10–12 min immediately after the pairing protocol with Δt =+10 ms, also resulted in robust conversion of acetylcholine-facilitated t-LTD into t-LTP, emulating the effect of dopamine (143 ± 17%, t(6) = 2.5, p=0.0447 vs. 100%, n = 7; Figure 2b,c; Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Dopamine can convert not only post-before-pre pairing-induced t-LTD but also acetylcholine-facilitated pre-before-post pairing-induced t-LTD into t-LTP, when acting within a few minutes following the induction protocol.
source: These results show that dopamine can convert not only post-before-pre pairing-induced t-LTD (Brzosko et al., 2015) but also acetylcholine-facilitated pre-before-post pairing-induced t-LTD into t-LTP, when acting within a few minutes following the induction protocol.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results in Figure 2 and previous work.

claim: The effect of dopamine is irrespective of the precise spike order and is mediated at least in part via the activation of the cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) signaling cascade.
source: The effect of dopamine is therefore irrespective of the precise spike order and is mediated at least in part via the activation of the cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) signaling cascade.
evidence: This is inferred from the forskolin experiment which activates the cAMP pathway.

claim: Acetylcholine did not have an effect on plasticity when applied after the induction protocol.
source: In contrast, acetylcholine did not have an effect on plasticity when applied after the induction protocol (Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Neuromodulation enables correlation-based synaptic plasticity, with dopamine promoting potentiation and acetylcholine facilitating depression.
source: At the synaptic level, our data emphasize three crucial features of neuromodulation of hippocampal STDP: (i) neuromodulation enables correlation-based synaptic plasticity, with dopamine promoting potentiation and acetylcholine facilitating depression (Figure 1);
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: Synaptic weights are not only graded in magnitude but also can shift polarity by subsequent neuromodulation.
source: (ii) synaptic weights are not only graded in magnitude but also can shift polarity by subsequent neuromodulation (Figures 1 and 2; Brzosko et al., 2015);
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: The conversion of synaptic depression into potentiation by dopamine can occur even after extended delay.
source: and (iii) the conversion of synaptic depression into potentiation by dopamine can occur even after extended delay (Figure 2; Brzosko et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: Sequential neuromodulation of hippocampal STDP is behaviorally relevant.
source: These characteristics suggest that sequential neuromodulation of hippocampal STDP is behaviorally relevant (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is inferred from the synaptic characteristics and tested in the computational model.

claim: Implementing the sequential modulation by acetylcholine and dopamine in the model led to a modest improvement in learning compared to control simulations during the initial reward learning phase.
source: During this initial reward learning phase, implementing the sequential modulation by acetylcholine and dopamine in the model led to a modest improvement in learning compared to control simulations (reward discovery: Figure 4aiii; successful trials: Figure 4aiv; time to reward: Figure 4av).
evidence: This is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 4.

claim: The functional advantage of cholinergic depression became evident when the reward location was moved to the opposite corner of the open field.
source: The functional advantage of cholinergic depression became evident in the second phase of the simulation, when the reward location was moved to the opposite corner of the open field (Figure 4bi).
evidence: This is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 4.

claim: Cholinergic depression enabled unlearning of the previously rewarded location, which led to enhanced exploration.
source: In this case, cholinergic depression enabled unlearning of the previously rewarded location (Figure 4bii), which led to enhanced exploration (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), thereby facilitating subsequent learning of the new reward location (Figure 4biii–v).
evidence: This is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 4.

claim: Decreasing the magnitude of dopaminergic potentiation resulted in slower learning.
source: Decreasing the magnitude of dopaminergic potentiation resulted in slower learning, while increasing it did not produce any statistically significant difference (Figure 4avi and Figure 4—figure supplement 2), probably due to a saturation effect.
evidence: This is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 4.

claim: Increasing the magnitude of acetylcholine effect yielded faster unlearning.
source: Altering the magnitude of cholinergic depression revealed a clear effect on unlearning performance, where increasing the magnitude of acetylcholine effect yielded faster unlearning (Figure 4bvi and Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 4.

claim: The concept of 'eligibility trace' is at the core of network models of reinforcement learning: it is both necessary and sufficient to learn causal associations between synaptic activity and delayed outcomes.
source: This concept of 'eligibility trace' is at the core of network models of reinforcement learning: it is both necessary and sufficient to learn causal associations between synaptic activity and delayed outcomes (Florian, 2007; Izhikevich, 2007; Legenstein et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous theoretical work.

claim: Neuromodulation converts classical STDP into a correlation-based rule, with same-sign weight changes for both pre-before-post and post-before-pre pairings.
source: Firstly, neuromodulation converts classical STDP into a correlation-based rule, with same-sign weight changes for both pre-before-post and post-before-pre pairings (Brzosko et al., 2015; this paper).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: It is the integral of the learning window that determines whether the agent learns (positive window) or unlearns (negative window).
source: This feature is incorporated into our model where, rather than the exact spike timing, it is the integral of the learning window (Figure 4—figure supplement 4) that determines whether the agent learns (positive window) or unlearns (negative window).
evidence: This is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: Cholinergic depression allows the agent to explicitly learn from unrewarded trials.
source: Secondly, cholinergic depression allows the agent to explicitly learn from unrewarded trials (this paper).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the computational modeling results.

claim: The sequentially neuromodulated synaptic learning rule, which allows the agent to learn from both rewarded and unrewarded actions, outperformed the model with symmetric dopamine-modulated learning window when the reward location was moved.
source: Our sequentially neuromodulated synaptic learning rule (test simulations), which allows the agent to learn from both rewarded (+ ACh + DA) and unrewarded actions (+ ACh – DA), outperformed both the model with symmetric dopamine-modulated learning window (– ACh + DA; Figure 3bi) and the standard reward modulated STDP model (Figure 4—figure supplement 4) when the reward location was moved.
evidence: This is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 4.

claim: Incorporating cholinergic depression allowed the agent to appropriately shift between learning and unlearning in a task-relevant manner.
source: Incorporating cholinergic depression allowed the agent to appropriately shift between learning and unlearning in a task-relevant manner.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the computational modeling results.

claim: A simple feed-forward network obeying cholinergic-dopaminergic sequential neuromodulation of STDP is sufficient to guide an agent to changing reward locations as required during natural foraging behavior.
source: Indeed, as demonstrated here, a simple feed-forward network obeying cholinergic-dopaminergic sequential neuromodulation of STDP is sufficient to guide an agent to changing reward locations as required during natural foraging behavior (Charnov, 1976; Stephens and Krebs, 1986).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the computational modeling results and supported by citations to work on foraging behavior.

claim: Muscarinic acetylcholine receptor activation during coordinated spiking activity biases STDP toward synaptic depression.
source: In conclusion, our findings demonstrate that muscarinic acetylcholine receptor activation during coordinated spiking activity biases STDP toward synaptic depression.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: The reward signal dopamine, via activation of the cAMP pathway, converts both conventional t-LTD and acetylcholine-facilitated synaptic depression into potentiation.
source: Meanwhile, the reward signal dopamine, via activation of the cAMP pathway, converts both conventional t-LTD (Brzosko et al., 2015) and acetylcholine-facilitated synaptic depression into potentiation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: Incorporating this synaptic learning rule into a simple feed-forward neural network model successfully guides the agent towards changing reward locations similar to natural foraging behavior.
source: Incorporating this synaptic learning rule into a simple feed-forward neural network model successfully guides the agent towards changing reward locations similar to natural foraging behavior.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the computational modeling results.

claim: Sequential neuromodulation of synaptic plasticity provides a robust biological mechanism that might be used in reward-based navigation and other hippocampus-dependent functions.
source: We suggest that sequential neuromodulation of synaptic plasticity provides a robust biological mechanism that might be used in reward-based navigation and other hippocampus-dependent functions.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion drawn from the experimental and computational results.

claim: Wild-type mice (C57BL/6; postnatal days 12–18) of both sexes were used in the experiments.
source: Wild-type mice (C57BL/6; RRID:IMSR_JAX:000664; postnatal days 12–18; from Harlan, Bicester, UK or Central Animal Facility, Cambridge University) of both sexes were housed on a 12 hr light/dark cycle at 19–23°C, with water and food ad libitum.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: Whole-cell patch-clamp recordings were made from CA1 pyramidal neurons.
source: Whole-cell patch-clamp recordings were made from CA1 pyramidal neurons (located adjacent to the stratum oriens).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: A monopolar stimulation electrode was placed in the stratum radiatum of the CA1 subfield for stimulation of Schaffer collaterals.
source: For stimulation of Schaffer collaterals, a monopolar stimulation electrode was placed in the stratum radiatum of the CA1 subfield.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: The plasticity induction protocol consisted of 100 pairings of a single EPSP followed by a single postsynaptic spike or a single postsynaptic spike followed by a single EPSP at 0.2 Hz.
